title: Starting a Fruit Wine Business | Craft Beer School
desc: How to build a fruit wine business: fruit sourcing, process, quality control, licences and a realistic route to the shelf.
teaser: Fruit wine can reach the shelf sooner than grape wine, but it has its own rules and its own quality traps.
standfirst: Fruit wine is made from fruits such as mango, jackfruit or pomegranate rather than grapes. Here is how to build a business around it, from fruit to licence to customer.
sections:
Fruit wine uses fruit that is already grown near you. Many fruits are cheaper or more available than wine grapes in some regions. Many fruit wines can be sold young, which shortens the cash cycle. The flavours can also be a clear point of difference on a shelf.

It is not easier, only different. Fruit wine needs as much care as grape wine. A bad batch costs the same.

There is a story too. A wine from a local fruit says something about place that a bought-in grape cannot. Tourists and gift buyers like a product tied to the region. Be careful not to overclaim. Describe the fruit and the process plainly and let the taste speak.

Quality starts with the fruit: ripe, sound and clean. Fruits differ from grapes in sugar and acid. Many contain less sugar than grapes, so winemakers often add sugar to reach a target alcohol. Some are high in acid and some are low, so acidity may need adjusting. Fruit with a lot of pectin can leave a hazy wine, so enzymes are often used to clear it.

Seasonality matters too. Fruit arrives in a short window. Plan to buy and process during the peak and to store pulp or juice safely if you will make wine later. Freezing or cold storage costs money but widens your production window.

The steps echo grape winemaking: prepare the fruit, extract juice or pulp, adjust sugar and acid, add yeast, ferment at a controlled temperature, rack, clarify, stabilise and bottle. Sulphur dioxide is a standard protection against spoilage and oxidation. Clean equipment and a lab to measure sugar, acid and pH are essential. Our guide on planning winery equipment covers the kit.

Learn the process properly before you sell. A cheap homemade method scaled up gives inconsistent wine. Consistency is what a buyer wants.

Fermentation temperature matters for fruit wine as for grape wine. Cool, steady fermentation holds aroma, while heat strips it. Yeast needs nutrients. Fruit musts are sometimes short of them, so winemakers add a nutrient to keep yeast healthy and avoid off flavours. Do trial batches of a few litres first, change one variable at a time and write everything down.
Know your customer and your category

Who will drink it? Fruit wine can suit people who find grape wine too dry or too complex. It may also fit gifts, festive meals and tourist shops. Check how the category is treated by law and by shops where you sell, because labelling and licensing for fruit wine can differ from grape wine.

Do the work in market research for a new wine brand before you commit to a flavour.

Taste against competitors. Buy the fruit wines already on the shelf and note sweetness, colour, strength and price. Many beginners make wines that are too sweet or too thin because they never compared. A blind tasting with a handful of honest tasters is cheap and useful.

Alcohol production needs licences everywhere. In India alcohol is a state subject, so the licence path for fruit wine, the label rules and the sale routes depend on your state and change over time. Other countries have their own systems. Ask the regulator or a licensing adviser at the start. See winery licensing steps.

Never sell before the licence is in place.

Fruit cost is a bigger share of the bill for some fruit wines than you may expect, because many fruits yield less juice per kilo than grapes and prices swing with the season. Work out how many bottles one kilo of fruit gives in your process, including losses. Then price the bottle from your full cost. See cost per bottle.

Aim for a short, clear range. One or two flavours made well beat six made badly. Taste each batch against a reference, record the results and keep samples.

Shelf life is another test. Fruit wines can change in bottle, so check stability, store samples at warm and cool temperatures and see how they hold up before you set a best-before period. Responsible marketing applies: no promotion aimed at minors.
faqs: Is fruit wine easier to make than grape wine?
Not easier. The fruit differs and so does the adjustment needed, but the discipline is the same.
Can I sell fruit wine as soon as it is made?
Many fruit wines are released young, but they still need to be stable and clear. Do not sell before the licence and testing are in place.
Which fruit should I start with?
The one you can source cleanly at a fair price and that people already enjoy.
Do fruit wines need different licences?
This depends on the country and, in India, the state. Ask the regulator.
